bib.title: Enabling Large Language Models to Generate Text with Citations

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Enabling Large Language Models to Generate Text with Citations" (ALCE). Tianyu Gao, Howard Yen, Jiatong Yu, Danqi Chen (Princeton). EMNLP 2023 main conference, pages 6465–6488. The venue is printed in the PDF header. arXiv 2305.14627.

COVERAGE: All 97,164 characters, 24 pages. I read the main text, the limitations and appendices A–I closely, including the full results Tables 19–21, the prompts and the examples. I only skimmed the reference list (pp. 10–13), for origins. The text extracted cleanly.

CLAIMS (most important first)
- claim: Even the best systems leave about half of ELI5 answers without full citation support.
  number: ~50%
  setup: ELI5 with the Sphere corpus and BM25, ChatGPT and GPT-4 VANILLA baselines, 2023 models.
  quote: "on the ELI5 dataset, around 50% generations of our ChatGPT and GPT-4 baselines are not fully supported by the cited passages"
  where: p.2. The abstract says "even the best models lack complete citation support 50% of the time".
- claim: Citation recall for a statement is 1 only if it has at least one citation and the cited passages, joined together, entail it according to an NLI model. A citation counts as "irrelevant" if it cannot support the statement alone and the other citations still support it without it. A citation can score precision 1 only when its statement has recall 1.
  number: none
  setup: TRUE, a T5-11B model fine-tuned on SNLI, MNLI, Fever, SciTail, PAWS and VitaminC. Statements are split at sentence boundaries, with at most 3 citations each. Passages are 100 words long.
  quote: "its citation recall is 1 if and only if there is at least one citation ( Ci ̸= ∅) and ϕ(concat(Ci), si) = 1" / "ci,j has a precision of 1 if si has recall =1 and ci,j is not irrelevant"
  where: p.4–5
- claim: The automatic citation metrics agree with human judges, more strongly for recall than for precision.
  number: kappa 0.698 (recall) and 0.525 (precision). Accuracy 85.1% and 77.6% against human labels.
  setup: Surge AI annotators, 100 sampled examples each from ASQA and ELI5, outputs from ChatGPT VANILLA, ChatGPT RERANK and Vicuna-13B.
  quote: "substantial agreement for citation recall (0.698) and moderate agreement for citation precision (0.525)" / "(85.1% for citation recall and 77.6% for citation precision)"
  where: p.9, App. G.5 p.17
- claim: The NLI metric over-flags irrelevant citations because it cannot recognise partial support.
  number: 75.6% recall and 66.1% precision at detecting irrelevant citations
  setup: Same human-evaluation sample.
  quote: "regarding detecting “irrelevant” citations, ALCE has a recall of 75.6% and a precision of 66.1%... it has a relatively high false positive rate"
  where: App. G.5 p.17
- claim: RERANK samples 4 answers and keeps the one with the best automatic citation recall. It raises citation quality, and human evaluation confirms the gain.
  number: ASQA recall 73.6→84.8, precision 72.5→81.6. ELI5 recall 51.1→69.3. Human ASQA recall 74.7→79.3.
  setup: ChatGPT gpt-3.5-turbo-0301, top-5 GTR (ASQA) or BM25 (ELI5) passages. RERANK was run on one seed only.
  quote: "w/ RERANK 77.0 40.2 84.8 81.6" (Table 4); "ChatGPT VANILLA 74.7 76.6 75.3 74.4 / w/ RERANK 79.3 81.9 83.9 80.8" (Table 8)
  where: p.6, p.9
- claim: Answering closed-book and adding citations afterwards (POST CITE) gives good correctness but poor citation quality.
  number: ASQA citation recall 26.7 against 73.6
  setup: ChatGPT. POST CITE matches each statement to its best passage among the top 100 using GTR.
  quote: "citation recall of CLOSED BOOK+POST CITE is lower than VANILLA by 47% on ASQA"
  where: p.7
- claim: The simple VANILLA prompt, which puts the top-k passages in context, is close to the best strategy. Interactive search during generation (INLINE SEARCH) does worse. Summaries and snippets raise correctness but lower citation quality on ASQA and ELI5.
  number: ASQA INLINE SEARCH 32.4 EM recall and 58.3 citation recall, against VANILLA 40.4 and 73.6
  setup: ChatGPT with a 4K context window, 2 demonstrations, 3 seeds.
  quote: "VANILLA (putting retrieved passages in context) achieves close-to-the-best performance among all prompting strategies."
  where: p.6
- claim: More passages in context do not help ChatGPT, but they do help GPT-4.
  number: GPT-4 ASQA EM recall 41.3 (5 passages) → 44.4 (20). ChatGPT-16K 36.1 → 36.1.
  setup: ASQA, GTR retriever, VANILLA prompt.
  quote: "correctness plateaus at top-1 passage and citation quality plateaus at top-3" / "GPT-4 is better at synthesizing information from its long context than ChatGPT"
  where: p.7–8, Table 7
- claim: Models' correctness falls short of what retrieval makes available, even when they are given gold passages.
  number: ASQA GTR recall@5 is 56.8. ChatGPT reaches 40.4 with the top 5 and 48.9 with 5 oracle passages.
  setup: The oracle passages are a greedy set of 5 chosen to match recall@100.
  quote: "top-5 retrieved passages can only cover 56.8% percent of the answers in ASQA" / "despite the presence of accurate answers in context, LLMs struggle to utilize them"
  where: p.5, p.8
- claim: The best open model, LLaMA-2-70B-Chat, matches ChatGPT on correctness but trails it on citation quality.
  number: ASQA 41.5 EM recall and 62.9/61.3 citation recall/precision
  setup: VANILLA prompt with 5 passages.
  quote: "Chat-70B (5-psg) 88.3 41.5 62.9 61.3"
  where: Table 4 p.6
- claim: ELI5 correctness is scored by "claim recall": text-davinci-003 writes 3 sub-claims from the gold answer, and TRUE checks which ones the output entails. The authors choose this over ROUGE-L.
  number: 93.33% of sub-claims judged faithful. The NLI step is 80.0% accurate.
  setup: 40 answers, 120 sub-claims, checked by the authors.
  quote: "112 out of the 120 (93.33%) sub-claims received a score of 1" / "the NLI model achieved an accuracy of 80.0%"
  where: App. A p.14
- claim: Each metric covers a shortcut the others would miss. Returning the top-1 passage scores near-perfect citations but low fluency. Returning its first 2 sentences scores near-perfect citations but low correctness.
  number: citation recall 99.4 and 98.7, MAUVE 20.8, EM recall 18.9
  setup: ASQA
  quote: "Top-1 passage 20.8 35.1 99.4 99.4 / First 2 sents 67.2 18.9 98.7 98.7"
  where: Table 11 p.15
- claim: A fine-tuned FiD (T5-base) model with POST CITE trails prompted ChatGPT on ASQA and does worse again on ELI5.
  number: ASQA EM recall 28.4 against 40.4
  quote: "FiD + POST CITE 75.8 28.4 58.1 58.0"
  where: Table 17 p.17

Benchmark setup: 1,000 dev-set examples each from ASQA (2018-12-20 Wikipedia, 21M passages), QAMPARI (same corpus, scored by recall-5) and ELI5 (Sphere, 899M passages). The benchmark has no training data. Retrieval uses GTR or DPR on Wikipedia and BM25 on Sphere, top 100. Decoding uses temperature 0.5 for OpenAI models and top_p 0.95 for open models.

LIMITS: The authors concede four things. (1) MAUVE depends on output length and is unstable. (2) ELI5 sub-claims may miss valid answers. (3) Citation quality is only as accurate as the NLI model, and because it cannot see "partial support" the automatic precision comes out lower than human precision. (4) The datasets leave out multi-hop, math and code questions. All methods are prompting only, with no training. They also show that the automatic scores are biased in RERANK's favour, since RERANK optimises the same metric.

The results date from 2023: ChatGPT-0301, GPT-4-0613, LLaMA-1/2, Vicuna and 2K–4K context windows. The context-length findings will not transfer to current long-context models. Statements are split at sentence level and nearly every sentence is assumed to need a citation. QAMPARI scores are all low (citation recall ≤27.4).

BUILDS ON: AIS framework (Rashkin et al., 2023); TRUE NLI (Honovich et al., 2022); attributed QA (Bohnet et al., 2022); WebGPT (Nakano et al., 2021) and GopherCite (Menick et al., 2022), described as the closest prior work; human evaluation of generative search engines (Liu et al., 2023); MAUVE (Pillutla et al., 2021); ASQA (Stelmakh et al., 2022), QAMPARI (Rubin et al., 2022), ELI5 (Fan et al., 2019), Sphere (Piktus et al., 2021); GTR (Ni et al., 2022) and DPR (Karpukhin et al., 2020); ReAct (Yao et al., 2023); FiD (Izacard and Grave, 2021); distraction by irrelevant context (Shi et al., 2023).

CODE: The VANILLA instruction is worth keeping. Table 23, p.21: "Write an accurate, engaging, and concise answer for the given question using only the provided search results (some of which might be irrelevant) and cite them properly. Use an unbiased and journalistic tone. Always cite for any factual claim. When citing several search results, use [1][2][3]. Cite at least one document and at most three documents in each sentence. If multiple documents support the sentence, only cite a minimum sufficient subset of the documents." Code repository: github.com/princeton-nlp/ALCE.

FIGURES: Figure 3, p.4, "Evaluation of citation quality... We use an NLI model to verify whether a statement is supported by its citations." This is the best candidate. One worked example shows recall 2/3 and precision 4/6, the leave-one-out test for an irrelevant citation, and the rule that recall 0 forces precision 0. That is much faster to grasp than the formal definition. Figure 4, p.8, is a second option: retrieval recall@k next to model correctness, which shows the ceiling retrieval sets.

AUDIT of citing passages
1. generative-ai/08-eval/notes/07-evaluating-rag-and-grounding.md:172 has three faults.
   - The note misdefines citation recall as "is every claim that needs a citation cited?". In ALCE, recall asks whether the statement is fully entailed by the cited passages taken together, and it requires at least one citation. That is a support test, not a coverage test.
   - Precision is roughly right but drops two conditions: a citation is penalised only if it fails alone AND is redundant given the others, and precision is gated on recall = 1.
   - "with a judge" is imprecise: ALCE uses an NLI model (TRUE, T5-11B), not an LLM judge.
   - "shows models citing irrelevant passages often" is a partial misattribution. The paper's headline is missing support (~50% on ELI5). It also warns that its irrelevance detector has a high false-positive rate (66.1% precision).
   - Suggested fix: carry the human agreement figures (kappa 0.698/0.525) and say the precision metric undercounts partial support.
   - Line 296, "Only citation precision and recall need a judge", is fine if "judge" covers an NLI model.
2. generative-ai/08-eval/notes/13-case-study-support-agent.md:182, "ALCE shows that even strong systems lack complete citation support". This is accurate but has no number or setup. It should read: about 50% of ChatGPT and GPT-4 answers on ELI5 (2023 models, BM25 over Sphere). On ASQA, citation recall was about 74% for ChatGPT. The bibliography entry at line 307 (EMNLP 2023) is correct.
3. generative-ai/02-rag-retrieval/notes/06-generation-for-rag.md:306, "Scores citation quality, correctness and fluency | For evaluating systems, not runtime". The first half is accurate. The second half is contradicted by the paper itself: RERANK uses ALCE's citation-recall NLI scorer at generation time (best of 4 samples), and humans confirmed it raised citation quality on ASQA and ELI5. The defensible limit is cost (4 generations plus a T5-11B NLI pass), not "not runtime".
   - Sharpens available: ALCE's finding that closed-book answers with post-hoc citations cut ASQA citation recall by 47 points directly supports the note's line 319, "Citation is not attribution". The plateau of ChatGPT at 1–3 passages could sharpen the FiD passage-count paragraph at line 217, which says it "says nothing about how a prompted LLM handles 100 chunks". ALCE tested up to 20 passages.
4. References rows. generative-ai/02-rag-retrieval/references.md:64 and generative-ai/08-eval/references.md:80 have no setup or claim, no EMNLP venue, and no PDF/✓ link, although the PDF exists at generative-ai/02-rag-retrieval/sources/gao-2023-enabling-large-language-models-generate.pdf. In 08-eval the row says "citation precision/recall", which is fine as a label.

I found no fabricated numbers in any citing passage. The problems are a wrong definition (recall), a claim the paper does not make ("not runtime"), and numbers given without their setup.

PROBLEMS:
- Text inside the figures extracts as fragments (Figures 2 and 3).
- The paper's own tables are inconsistent in places. Table 11 lists ChatGPT ASQA citation precision as 63.0 against 72.5 elsewhere. The INLINE SEARCH row of Table 19 has shifted columns (ROUGE-L 58.2). Table 21 contains the typo "(2.w)".
- SUMM/CLOSED BOOK ELI5 numbers differ slightly between the main and full tables (40.3/40.2, 15.5/15.4).
- The PDF contains no embedded instructions.
- I wrote a temporary text dump to /tmp/alce.txt for reading. I edited no repo files.
